passage: Every evening at the bus stop, the same boy from her tuition class, Yusuf, stood far too close to Reena, even when there was plenty of room. Reena stepped back. He stepped forward. She turned sideways and put her school bag between them. He kept talking anyway. Her heart was pounding. She wanted to leave but didn't want to make a scene. She looked for the shopkeeper opposite, walked over to buy water and stayed there until the bus came. That night she told her father. He listened and said, "You did well to step away. We'll speak to the tuition teacher tomorrow."

qa.q: What did Reena put between herself and Yusuf?
qa.a: She put her school bag between them.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when Yusuf kept stepping closer?
qa.a: She was uneasy and scared, and her heart was pounding. She wanted to leave without making a scene.

qa.q: What should a teenager do if someone keeps closing in or ignores clear signals?
qa.a: Step away, put distance or an object between them, go to a safe place and tell a trusted adult. Reena told her father.

qa.q: How might Reena's father have felt hearing about it?
qa.a: He listened and took her seriously, and decided to speak to the teacher. He reassured her that stepping away was right.

grounding: A teenager steps back and puts a bag between herself and someone standing too close, and tells an adult.

passage:
"Mehak, you're quiet," said Sonali, putting down her pen.
"There's a boy in my batch. He stands right next to me at the gate, and then he walks behind me."
"Do you want that?"
"No! I keep stepping away, but he doesn't stop."
"Then it isn't fine. Have you said anything?"
"I turned my back and held my folder in front of me."
"That's smart. But now we tell someone: your mother, and the tuition teacher."
Mehak swallowed. "I thought it was my fault."
"It isn't." Sonali reached over. "Can I hold your hand while we go?" Mehak nodded.

qa.q: Where does the boy stand next to Mehak?
qa.a: He stands right next to her at the gate.

qa.q: What is Mehak feeling about the boy, and what does she say about fault?
qa.a: She is uncomfortable and scared, and she thought it was her fault. Her stepping away and holding her folder show she doesn't want the closeness.

qa.q: What should Mehak and Sonali do next?
qa.a: Tell a trusted adult like Mehak's mother and the tuition teacher, since he keeps closing in. Her discomfort is valid.

qa.q: How does Sonali see the situation?
qa.a: She takes it seriously, tells Mehak it isn't her fault and asks before holding her hand. She wants to help her.

grounding: A teenager steps away and uses an object as a barrier when someone stands too close, and tells adults.

passage:
In Class 10, a boy at my coaching centre, Vijay, started standing too close to me after class. At first I thought it was an accident. But every day he'd lean in, and when I stepped back, he'd step forward again.
I started holding my bag in front of me, like a wall. I turned away when he talked. He didn't stop. One evening, he followed me all the way to the bus stop, walking right behind me.
That night I told my father. He didn't say, "Maybe you misunderstood." He said, "You did the right thing telling me."
The next day, he came with me to the coaching centre and spoke to the director. After that, Vijay was moved to a different batch, and my father picked me up for the next month.
- Gopika

qa.q: What did Gopika hold in front as a wall?
qa.a: The bag.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when Vijay kept stepping closer?
qa.a: Gopika felt uneasy and unsafe, especially when he ignored the stepping back and followed to the bus stop.

qa.q: What did Gopika do that was wise?
qa.a: Gopika stepped back, used the bag as a barrier, turned away, and told the father the same night when Vijay kept closing in.

qa.q: How did Gopika's father respond?
qa.a: He believed Gopika, said telling him was right, and went to the coaching director the next day.

grounding: The narrator recalls stepping away and using a bag as a barrier when someone kept closing in, and telling a trusted adult.

passage:
Library note, Tuesday
Over the last week I've noticed Naveen, a Class 8 student, repeatedly stepping away from an older boy in the library. When the older boy sits next to him, Naveen shifts his chair or puts his backpack between them. Today the older boy followed Naveen from the history shelf to the science shelf and stood right behind him.
I asked Naveen to help me return some books, and in the storeroom I asked him quietly if he was okay.
He said the older boy keeps standing too close and following him, even after Naveen tells him to stop.
I told Naveen he was right to feel uncomfortable and right to tell me. This afternoon I spoke to his class teacher and the counsellor, and the older boy has been spoken to.
- Ms Maria, librarian

qa.q: What did Naveen put between himself and the older boy?
qa.a: His backpack.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when the older boy followed him?
qa.a: Naveen felt uncomfortable and uneasy, trying to protect his space by stepping away and using his backpack.

qa.q: What did Ms Maria do that helped Naveen?
qa.a: She noticed the pattern, asked privately, told Naveen his feelings were valid, and acted that afternoon with the class teacher and counsellor.

qa.q: How might the older boy see the library now?
qa.a: The older boy will likely know adults are watching and that he must respect others' space.

grounding: A librarian's note shows a teenager stepping away from someone who keeps closing in, and an adult acting the same day.

passage:
Saturday
At the Losar festival in the monastery courtyard, a man kept standing right behind me in the crowd. When I moved forward, he moved too. When I stepped left, he stepped left. I could feel his breath on my neck.
I turned sideways and held my shawl bundled in front of me. He still didn't back off.
I pushed through to where Jasleen and her mother were standing near the prayer wheels. I whispered to Aunty what was happening.
She put her arm around me, looked straight at the man, and said loudly, "Please give us space." Then she took me to the volunteers at the gate and told them. They walked over, and he left.
I'm glad I didn't just stay quiet.
- Pema

qa.q: Where were Jasleen and her mother standing?
qa.a: Near the prayer wheels.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when the man kept following in the crowd?
qa.a: Pema felt uneasy and scared, sensing the man was ignoring clear signals to back off.

qa.q: What did Pema do that was right?
qa.a: Pema turned sideways, used the shawl as a barrier, moved to a trusted adult, and told her.

qa.q: How did Jasleen's mother respond to Pema?
qa.a: She kept Pema close, told the man firmly to give space, and reported him to the volunteers straight away.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows stepping away from someone who keeps closing in at a festival and telling an adult who acts at once.
